title: How would you design a real-time chat / messaging system (e.g. WhatsApp/Slack) — why persist the message to the DB BEFORE delivering it, WebSockets (full-duplex) vs long-polling for delivery, guaranteeing per-conversation message ordering, delivery vs read receipts, presence/typing indicators, offline users (queue + push notification), multi-device sync, and how do you scale stateful WebSocket servers (sticky sessions / a shared pub-sub like Redis so a message published on one server reaches a socket on another)?
shortTitle: How would you design a real-time chat / messaging system like WhatsApp or Slack

s1_definition.profdef: A real-time chat system accepts a message, persists it durably before acknowledging and delivering it, then pushes it to recipients over a full-duplex WebSocket connection, falling back to a queue plus push notification for offline users. It guarantees per-conversation ordering with a monotonic sequence per conversation, tracks delivery and read receipts as separate state transitions, maintains presence and typing indicators as ephemeral signals, syncs across a user's multiple devices, and scales its stateful WebSocket servers by using sticky sessions plus a shared pub-sub layer such as Redis so a message arriving on one server can reach a recipient's socket held open on another.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's secure messaging where Rajesh chats with his relationship manager Priya. When Rajesh sends a message, the bank first writes it in the permanent ledger (database) and only then says "sent", so even if the line drops, the message is never lost. If Priya is online, a dedicated open phone line (WebSocket) delivers it instantly both ways. If Priya is away, the message waits in her inbox (queue) and her phone buzzes (push notification). The bank stamps each message with a running number per conversation so they always appear in the right order, shows ticks for delivered and read, and if Priya reads it on her tablet, her laptop updates too (multi-device sync).
s1_definition.oneliner: Persist first then deliver, use WebSockets for live full-duplex delivery with a Redis pub-sub fan-out across servers, order per conversation with a sequence number, and fall back to queue plus push for offline users.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A real-time chat system accepts a message, persists it durably before acknowledging and delivering it, then pushes it to recipients over a full-duplex WebSocket connection, falling back to a queue plus push notification for offline users. It guarantees per-conversation ordering with a monotonic sequence per conversation, tracks delivery and read receipts as separate state transitions, maintains presence and typing indicators as ephemeral signals, syncs across a user's multiple devices, and scales its stateful WebSocket servers by using sticky sessions plus a shared pub-sub layer such as Redis so a message arriving on one server can reach a recipient's socket held open on another.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's secure messaging where Rajesh chats with his relationship manager Priya. When Rajesh sends a message, the bank first writes it in the permanent ledger (database) and only then says "sent", so even if the line drops, the message is never lost. If Priya is online, a dedicated open phone line (WebSocket) delivers it instantly both ways. If Priya is away, the message waits in her inbox (queue) and her phone buzzes (push notification). The bank stamps each message with a running number per conversation so they always appear in the right order, shows ticks for delivered and read, and if Priya reads it on her tablet, her laptop updates too (multi-device sync).

**One line to remember:** Persist first then deliver, use WebSockets for live full-duplex delivery with a Redis pub-sub fan-out across servers, order per conversation with a sequence number, and fall back to queue plus push for offline users.

sections.s2_technical:
Why persist before delivering. The message must be written to durable storage and get an acknowledged, assigned sequence before you tell the sender it is sent and before you push it to recipients. If you deliver first and persist later, a crash between the two loses the message even though the sender saw "sent", and recipients who were briefly offline never get it because there is no record to replay. Persist-first makes the database the source of truth: delivery is just a projection of what is already stored, and any missed delivery is recovered by re-reading from storage. The sender's acknowledgment means durably stored, not merely delivered.

WebSockets versus long-polling. HTTP is request-response, so for the server to push a message to a client the client would have to keep asking. Long-polling fakes push by holding a request open until there is data, then the client immediately re-requests; it works but is wasteful and higher latency. WebSockets upgrade the connection to a persistent, full-duplex channel where server and client send frames to each other any time without re-establishing. For chat, where the server must push messages, typing indicators, and presence instantly in both directions, WebSockets are the right transport. Long-polling remains a useful fallback where WebSockets are blocked.

Per-conversation ordering. Users expect messages within a conversation to appear in the order sent. You assign each message a monotonically increasing sequence number scoped to its conversation, generated at persist time, for example by an atomic counter per conversation or a database sequence. Clients render by sequence, not arrival time, so even if the network reorders delivery, the display order is correct. You do not need a global order across all conversations, only within each one, which is far cheaper to guarantee.

Delivery versus read receipts. These are two distinct states. Delivered means the message reached the recipient's device; read means the user actually opened it. You model them as state transitions on the message per recipient: SENT, then DELIVERED when the recipient's client acknowledges receipt, then READ when the client reports the user viewed it. The recipient's client sends small acknowledgment events back over the WebSocket, and the sender's client updates the ticks. In group chats you track this per member.

Presence and typing indicators. These are ephemeral, high-churn signals, not durable messages. Presence (online/offline/last-seen) and typing ("Priya is typing...") are published to a fast in-memory store and fanned out to interested clients, and they expire quickly. You do not persist every keystroke; typing is a short-lived event with a timeout. Keeping these out of the durable message path keeps the database light.

Offline users: queue plus push. If a recipient has no live WebSocket, you cannot push over a socket. The message is already persisted, so you enqueue a delivery task and send a mobile push notification through APNs or FCM to wake the device. When the user comes back online, the client reconnects, tells the server its last-seen sequence per conversation, and the server replays everything newer from storage, so no message is lost.

Multi-device sync. A user may be on phone, tablet, and laptop at once. Each device holds its own WebSocket and its own last-seen sequence per conversation. A new message fans out to all of the user's live devices, and read state syncs across them: reading on the tablet marks it read everywhere. This is why read receipts are tracked server-side per user and broadcast to that user's other devices.

Scaling stateful WebSocket servers. WebSockets are stateful: a user's socket lives on one specific server. With many servers behind a load balancer, Rajesh's socket might be on server A while the message from Priya arrives on server B. Server B has no direct socket to Rajesh. Two mechanisms solve this. Sticky sessions keep a given user pinned to the same server for the life of the connection, so reconnections land consistently. And a shared pub-sub layer, typically Redis pub-sub or a message bus, lets server B publish the message to a channel for Rajesh, which server A, holding his socket, is subscribed to and delivers. So every server publishes outbound messages to the pub-sub, and each server delivers to the local sockets it owns. This decouples "which server received it" from "which server holds the recipient's socket."

The senior nuance is idempotency and exactly-once feel. Networks retry, so a client may send the same message twice; you dedupe with a client-generated message ID so the same logical message is stored once. Delivery is at-least-once with client-side dedupe by message ID, which gives an exactly-once experience without the impossible cost of true exactly-once delivery.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India offers secure in-app chat between customers and relationship managers. Rajesh (SAV2001) chats with Priya (CUR3001), his relationship manager, about a loan.

Problem 1 — messages were lost on a crash. The old design pushed the message to Priya first and wrote to the database afterward, so a crash in between lost messages that Rajesh had already seen marked "sent". This is why we persist first and only then deliver.

Problem 2 — messages appeared out of order. Two quick messages from Rajesh sometimes showed in the wrong order because display used arrival time. This is why each message gets a per-conversation sequence number and clients render by sequence.

Problem 3 — when Priya was on another server, Rajesh's message never reached her. Her WebSocket was on server A, Rajesh's message landed on server B, and B had no socket to her. This is why we fan out through a shared Redis pub-sub so any server can reach any socket.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the server-side core: a `Message` with a per-conversation sequence, a `MessageStore` (persist-first source of truth), a `SequenceGenerator` per conversation, a `ConnectionRegistry` of live sockets per user per server, a `PubSub` fan-out simulating Redis, and a `ChatService` that persists then delivers, handling an offline recipient via a queue and tracking delivery and read receipts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya connects on serverA, Rajesh on serverB (different servers). Rajesh sends two messages, Priya reads them, goes offline, Rajesh sends a third, Priya reconnects.

Step 1: Rajesh sends "Hi Priya" (lands on serverB). ChatService gets sequence 1 from the generator and persists the message to the store first. Only then does it publish to channel user:CUR3001.

Step 2: serverA, holding Priya's socket, is subscribed to user:CUR3001 through the shared pub-sub, so even though the message arrived on serverB, serverA receives the publish and pushes it down Priya's WebSocket. Priya sees seq=1. This is the cross-server fan-out.

Step 3: Rajesh's second message gets sequence 2, persisted, published, delivered. Because clients render by sequence, the two always appear in order even if the network reordered them.

Step 4: Priya reads both. markRead updates the stored messages to READ up to seq 2 and the read receipt syncs to Rajesh's devices, turning his ticks blue.

Step 5: Priya disconnects (serverA unsubscribes her channel). Rajesh sends "interest rate?" with sequence 3. It is persisted, but no live socket receives the publish, so the fallback enqueues it and sends a push notification to wake Priya's phone.

Step 6: Priya reconnects on serverA with last-seen sequence 2. replayMissed reads everything with sequence greater than 2 from the store, finds message 3, and delivers it. No message was lost because it was persisted before delivery.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] PERSISTED SAV2001:CUR3001 seq=1 from SAV2001
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] → Priya device sees: [seq=1] SAV2001: "Hi Priya, about my home loan"
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] PERSISTED SAV2001:CUR3001 seq=2 from SAV2001
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] → Priya device sees: [seq=2] SAV2001: "What documents do you need?"
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] READ receipt: CUR3001 read up to seq 2 → sync to sender's devices
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] PERSISTED SAV2001:CUR3001 seq=3 from SAV2001
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] REPLAY 1 missed messages to CUR3001 from seq > 2
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] → Priya device sees (replay): [seq=3] SAV2001: "Also, what is the interest rate?"
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh (socket on serverB) sends "Hi Priya"
    │
    ▼
  ChatService
    │ seq.next(convo) → 1
    │ STEP 1: store.persist(msg)   ← DURABLE FIRST (source of truth)
    │ STEP 2: pubSub.publish("user:CUR3001", msg)
    ▼
  Redis pub-sub channel "user:CUR3001"
    │ serverA is subscribed (Priya's socket lives there)
    ▼
  serverA → Priya's WebSocket → "[seq=1] Hi Priya"

  ── Ordering ──  clients render by seq (1,2,3), not arrival time

  ── Read receipt ──
  Priya reads → markRead(upTo=2) → store state=READ → publish to Rajesh's devices

  ── Offline ──
  Priya disconnects → send seq=3 → no live socket
      │ persisted already
      ▼
  OfflineQueue.enqueue + PushNotifier(FCM) → phone buzzes

  ── Reconnect / replay ──
  Priya reconnects, lastSeen=2 → store.since(convo, 2) → [seq=3] → deliver
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I design a real-time chat system around one rule above all: persist the message to durable storage and assign its sequence before I acknowledge the sender or deliver it to anyone. If I deliver first and persist later, a crash in between loses a message the sender already saw marked sent, and an offline recipient has nothing to replay. Persist-first makes the database the source of truth, so delivery is just a projection of what is already stored and any missed delivery is recovered by re-reading. On my project at National Bank of India this fixed a real bug where customer messages to relationship managers were lost on a crash.

For the live transport I use WebSockets rather than long-polling, because chat needs the server to push messages, typing indicators, and presence instantly in both directions, and a WebSocket is a persistent full-duplex channel that does exactly that, whereas long-polling fakes push by repeatedly holding and re-issuing requests, which is wasteful and higher latency, so I keep it only as a fallback. I guarantee ordering per conversation, not globally, by assigning each message a monotonically increasing sequence number scoped to its conversation at persist time, and clients render by sequence rather than arrival time, so even if the network reorders delivery the display order is always correct.

I model delivery and read as two separate state transitions per recipient: sent, then delivered when the recipient's client acknowledges receipt, then read when the user actually opens it, with the recipient's client sending small acknowledgment events back over the socket so the sender's ticks update. Presence and typing I treat as ephemeral high-churn signals kept in a fast in-memory store with short expiry, never in the durable message path, because I do not persist every keystroke. For offline users, since the message is already stored, I enqueue a delivery task and send a mobile push through FCM or APNs to wake the device, and when the user reconnects their client tells me its last-seen sequence per conversation and I replay everything newer from storage, so nothing is lost. Multi-device sync falls out of this naturally: each device has its own socket and last-seen sequence, a message fans out to all of a user's live devices, and read state syncs across them.

The hardest scaling problem is that WebSockets are stateful, so a user's socket lives on one specific server, and a message may arrive on a different server that has no socket to the recipient. I solve this two ways: sticky sessions pin a user to the same server for the life of the connection, and a shared pub-sub layer like Redis lets the server that received the message publish it to a per-user channel that the server holding the recipient's socket is subscribed to, so it delivers locally. That decouples which server received the message from which server holds the recipient's socket, which is exactly how I fixed messages failing when sender and recipient were on different servers. I also dedupe by a client-generated message ID so retries store the message once, giving an exactly-once experience over at-least-once delivery.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I persist first so the database is the source of truth, deliver live over full-duplex WebSockets with a Redis pub-sub fan-out and sticky sessions so any server can reach any socket, order strictly per conversation with a sequence number, track delivery and read as separate receipts synced across a user's devices, and fall back to a durable queue plus push notification with on-reconnect replay so an offline user never misses a message.
